Assume the shaft is solid, circular, prismatic, and made of a homogeneous isotropic linear-elastic material with constant shear modulus G.
Assume the torque T is constant over the shaft length L and the applied torque produces uniform torsion.
Assume the angle-of-twist limit phi_allow is the maximum allowable total angle of twist over the full length L.
Assume the length L is large compared with the diameter so that transverse shear deformation is negligible for the twist calculation.
Assume warping of the cross-section is free and not restrained.
The polar second moment of area of a solid circular shaft of diameter d is J = pi d^4 / 32.
The governing angle-of-twist relation is phi = T L / (G J).
The required diameter from the angle-of-twist limit is d = (32 T L / (pi G phi_allow))^(1/4).
The angle of twist per unit length is theta = phi / L = T / (G J).
If the limit is given as an allowable twist per unit length theta_allow, use phi_allow = theta_allow L.
The maximum torsional shear stress is tau_torsion,max = T (d/2) / J = 16 T / (pi d^3).
If a transverse shear force V is also present, the maximum transverse shear stress in a solid circular cross-section is tau_transverse,max = 4 V / (3 A) = 16 V / (3 pi d^2).
Transverse shear stress does not affect the angle-of-twist calculation for a slender shaft.
Torsional shear stress is maximum at the outer surface, while transverse shear stress is maximum at the center, so do not simply add the two maximum values at one point.
If a material shear stress limit is specified, check that the relevant shear stress at the critical location does not exceed the allowable value.
Use consistent units for T, L, G, and phi_allow, and round the final computed diameter up to the next available standard size.
